summary: Defines a syntax for representing both GSTN (the global telephone network) addresses and Internet addresses in one place, for email services that mix the two such as fax over email. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Some mail goes to a phone number rather than a mailbox. This gives a way to write both kinds of address together.

how do fax gateways use email addresses
subtitle: How to write telephone and fax numbers, subaddresses, names and postal details inside an e-mail address.

tldr.problem: The minimal format for putting a telephone-network (GSTN) address inside an e-mail address could not express local numbering schemes, subaddresses, post-dial sequences or the name and postal details of a sender or recipient.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2846 extends the minimal syntax from RFC 2303 with local-phone numbers, an ISDN subaddress, a post-dial sequence and an optional pstn-recipient made of a name plus qualifiers, all defined in ABNF.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 3191 and RFC 3192, and it sets up IANA registration for new service selectors and qualifiers.

facts.value: 10 (ORG, OFNO, OFNA, STR, ADDR, ADDU, ADDL, POB, ZIP, CO)

today: RFC 2846 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000 and is updated by RFC 3191 and RFC 3192. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why GSTN Addresses Need Extending
sections.content:
The Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN, also known as the Public Switched Telephone Network or PSTN) has addresses that range from a bare number to a large, complex collection of elements. RFC 2303 defined a minimal way to carry such an address inside an Internet e-mail address and a mechanism for adding more elements. RFC 2846 uses that mechanism to define the full syntax, and it holds the IANA registrations for the new elements.

The new elements cover detailed phone number formats (gstn-phone, sub-addr-spec and post-dial) and a way to describe the message originator or recipient (pstn-recipient). Other specifications MAY add further elements, such as the T33S element in RFC 2304, but they MUST use the definitions in this memo for the elements it covers.

The syntax is written in ABNF, and the RFC kept compatibility with the MIXER gateway specification (RFC 2156) where it could. It notes that some elements can also be reused outside e-mail, for example in URLs.
sections.eli5: A phone number alone is sometimes not enough, like a letter that needs a flat number and a name. This RFC adds the extra pieces to the simple version that came before.

sections.title: Extended Phone Numbers
sections.content:
The minimal format only allowed a global-phone number, which starts with +. RFC 2846 adds local-phone for numbering schemes where that does not apply. The combined element is gstn-phone = ( global-phone / local-phone ), and a pstn-mbox is now a service selector, an equals sign and a phone number, optionally followed by a subaddress and a post-dial sequence.

A local-phone is an optional exit-code followed by an optional dial-number. The exit code can hold things such as the digit to reach an outside line, a long distance carrier code or an access password. Both parts are a phone-string, built from DTMF characters (the digits, the hash and star keys, and the letters A to D), a pause p, a tone wait w and the written separators (hyphen and full stop). The DTMF letters are only for DTMF dialling, not the letters printed on some phone keypads.

The + character is reserved for global numbers and MUST NOT start a local-phone string. The meaning of p and w depends on the MTA implementation, and both are case insensitive. A local-phone number should be used only by the destination MTA named by mta-I-pstn; other MTAs should pass the message on without changing the left-hand side of the address.
sections.eli5: Some phone numbers work only from one place, like a short code inside your school. This adds a way to write those, including little signals such as wait here or pause.

sections.title: Subaddresses, Post-Dial Digits and Multiple Recipients
sections.content:
Some telephone services need a subaddress to find the final destination. This RFC defines the ISDN one: sub-addr-spec = [ isdn-sep isub-addr ], where the separator is /ISUB= (case insensitive) and the value is digits, optionally with written separators. The fax T.33 subaddress is defined in RFC 2304 instead.

Sometimes more dialling is needed after the connection is made, for example to move through an automated menu with DTMF tones. The post-sep element /POSTD= (also case insensitive) followed by a post-dial phone-string handles that.

When a destination needs several subaddresses, e-mail practice still uses one unique address per recipient, so multiple pstn-mbox elements are REQUIRED. A user agent MAY accept several subaddresses for one global-phone, but it MUST generate multiple pstn-mbox elements when it submits the message to the MTA.
sections.eli5: It is like calling a company and then dialling an extension, or pressing buttons in a phone menu. These parts of the address say which extension and which buttons.

sections.title: The pstn-recipient
sections.content:
Gateways often need more than a number. An offramp fax gateway, for example, could print the intended recipient on a fax cover page, and could qualify the cover page headers with the originator's details. The optional pstn-recipient element carries this. To keep the syntax compact, the same element works for the originator as well as the recipient.

It is an optional recipient-name followed by any number of recipient-qualifier elements, and the extended address becomes pstn-mbox [ pstn-recipient ] [ qualif-type1 ]. The name is written as /ATTN= and then a personal name made of an optional given name, optional initials and a required surname, separated by dots. Initials may be several letters, so a person with several given names can have them all represented.

The whole pstn-address MUST follow the quoting rules of the relevant e-mail standards, RFC 822 and RFC 1123.
sections.eli5: This is the name on the envelope. A fax machine can print it on the cover page so the right person gets the paper.

sections.title: Qualifiers for Physical Delivery
sections.content:
A name is sometimes not enough. The recipient-qualifier is either a qualif-type1 (from RFC 2303, in the form /keyword=string) or a new qualif-type2, written /label=string. Type 2 exists for items beyond what type 1 covers, and its label is one of ten values: ORG, OFNO, OFNA, STR, ADDR, ADDU, ADDL, POB, ZIP and CO.

One or a few of them are usually enough to identify someone exactly. Because the total length of the address MUST NOT exceed the limits in the e-mail standards, only the strictly needed elements SHOULD be used.

The meanings come from the ITU F.401 specification, but the labels are deliberately named differently to avoid a conflict with X.400 addressing. Specifications that define new qualif-type1 elements are cautioned to avoid labels that overlap with F.401.
sections.eli5: These are the extra lines on a postal address: company, office, street, post box, zip code and country. You only write the ones you really need.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows a set of examples, noting they are for illustration only. A fax number in Italy dialled from the USA is written FAX=0103940226338. A hypothetical XYZ service in Germany with an ISDN subaddress looks like XYZ=+49.81.7856345/ISUB=1234. A fax number can also add a T.33 subaddress and a post-dial sequence: FAX=+1-202-455-7622/T33S=8745/PostD=p1w7005393w373.

Names follow the same pattern. /ATTN=Carlo.CMLS.Nascimento uses the complete set of initials for a person whose given names are Carlo Maria Luis Santo. Adding @faxgw, where faxgw is the mta-I-pstn field, turns an address into a complete pstn-email. The RFC also walks through a full SMTP transaction that sends a MIME message with a TIFF fax body part to a FAX= address.
sections.eli5: The examples are like sample addresses on a form. They show how a phone number, an extension and a name fit together on one line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
E-mail routing depends on DNS data, so a successful attack on DNS could send messages through an MTA or gateway whose software has been compromised. Attackers could compromise a DNS server, forge a response or return incorrect additional information. Clients SHOULD base mail routing only on authoritative answers and, once DNS Security becomes more widely deployed, SHOULD use it to verify mail routing records.

There is a second risk specific to this memo. Some GSTN services need private codes such as personal identification numbers. Because e-mail addresses cross MTAs without encoding, these codes inside a local-phone number could be read by others, and might even be printed on fax cover pages. Senders SHOULD be given ways to prevent this, such as code encryption or masquerading, with out-of-band authorization or encrypted special fields named as the available non-standard techniques.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks a fake map into the mail system, letters could be sent the wrong way. Also, a secret code written in an address could be read by anyone who handles the letter.

sections.title: IANA Registration of Services and Qualifiers
sections.content:
Because service selectors and qualif-type1 keywords are extensible, new values MUST be registered with IANA. Every registration MUST meet the Specification Required rule of RFC 2434: the values and their meaning must be documented in an RFC or another permanent, readily available reference in enough detail for independent implementations to interoperate. IANA MUST NOT accept registrations that lack such a specification or do not fully follow the template forms.

The appendices give the two form templates and the filled-in forms for the elements defined here: the FAX service selector, the ISDN subaddress, the post-dial elements, the recipient name and the ten physical delivery qualifiers.
sections.eli5: There is one official list of allowed words, kept by a librarian. To add a new word, you first have to write down clearly what it means.
